wonders.story: Old computers had very little memory, so programmers saved space by writing years with two digits: 1975 became 75. This worked for decades. But in the year 2000 the date would become 00, and many programs might think it was 1900. Calculations with dates, such as ages or bills, could go wrong. This was the Year 2000 problem, or Y2K. Around the world, programmers spent years checking and fixing old code, and one estimate says over 300 billion US dollars was spent. On 1 January 2000, only small things broke. A newborn baby in Denmark was recorded as 100 years old, and one website showed the year 19100. Because so little happened, some people said the danger had been exaggerated. Others call this the preparedness paradox (প্রস্তুতির ধাঁধা - when good preparation makes a danger look unreal).
also: A similar problem is coming: some systems that count time in a 32-bit number will run out on 19 January 2038.
Experts still argue about how much of the Y2K spending was really needed.
Police breathalysers in Hong Kong stopped working at midnight on 1 January 2000.
wonders.think: If a disaster is prevented, how can anyone prove it would have happened?

wonders.title: A rocket exploded because a big number did not fit in a small box
wonders.story: On 4 June 1996, Europe's new Ariane 5 rocket made its first flight. About 37 seconds later, it turned off course and destroyed itself. There was no attack. It was a bug. Part of the guidance software was copied from the older, slower Ariane 4. It turned a speed value from a large number format (64-bit) into a small one (16-bit). On Ariane 4, the number always fitted. Ariane 5 was faster, so the number was too big: an overflow (ওভারফ্লো - when a number is too big for its space). The computer stopped with an error. The backup computer ran the same code, so it failed in the same way. The loss was more than 370 million US dollars. The inquiry's lessons: test with real data for the new machine, and never assume old code is safe in a new place.
also: The rocket was carrying four science satellites called Cluster.
The faulty part of the code was not even needed after the rocket left the ground.
Replacement Cluster satellites were launched in 2000 on Russian Soyuz rockets.
wonders.think: When you reuse something that worked before, what questions should you ask first?

wonders.title: Log4Shell: when writing down a message could hand over a server
wonders.story: Most big programs keep a log, a diary of what happens: who logged in, which errors appeared. Many Java programs use a free tool called Log4j to write these logs. In November 2021, Chen Zhaojun of the Alibaba Cloud security team privately warned Log4j's volunteer developers about a serious flaw. Log4j had a helpful feature: if a log message contained a special pattern, Log4j would look something up, even from another server on the internet. So if an attacker could get special text into a log, the server might download and run the attacker's code. The flaw became public in December 2021 and got the highest danger score, 10 out of 10. The defence: fast updates, and knowing every dependency (নির্ভরশীল অংশ - a borrowed part your program is built from) inside your software.
also: Its official ID is CVE-2021-44228.
Log4j is looked after by volunteers at the Apache Software Foundation.
One study found that 93% of large companies' cloud systems were affected.
wonders.think: Should a tool do helpful extra things automatically, or only exactly what it is told?

wonders.title: Half a second of delay revealed a hidden backdoor in Linux
wonders.story: In March 2024, Andres Freund, a software developer at Microsoft, noticed something small. On his Linux test computer, logging in with SSH used too much processor power and took about half a second longer than before. Most people would not care. He investigated. He found that xz, a free compression tool used by many Linux systems, had a hidden backdoor (ব্যাকডোর - a secret way in) in its newest versions, 5.6.0 and 5.6.1. Someone using the name Jia Tan had spent over two years helping the project and earning trust, until they could add code. Fake accounts had also pressured the original maintainer to accept help. Freund reported it publicly on 29 March 2024. Because he noticed early, the bad versions had not reached most stable Linux systems. The lesson: measure, notice, and look after the volunteers who maintain free software.
also: The backdoor's ID is CVE-2024-3094, with the highest danger score of 10.
Freund described himself as not a security researcher; he was checking performance.
Stable Ubuntu, which Linux Mint is built on, did not get the bad versions.
wonders.think: Freund noticed half a second. What small strange thing on your own computer would you investigate?

wonders.title: An AI found a hidden bug in real software before anyone was hurt
wonders.story: In October 2024, an AI system called Big Sleep found a memory bug in SQLite. SQLite is a small database that runs inside phones, browsers and countless apps. Big Sleep was built by Google Project Zero, a team that hunts for unknown flaws, together with Google DeepMind. The AI studied the code and tested its ideas, like a human researcher. The SQLite developers fixed the bug on the same day it was reported, before it reached an official release, so no users were affected. Google said it believed this was the first public example of an AI finding an unknown, exploitable (কাজে লাগানো যায় এমন - usable by an attacker) memory bug in widely used real software. In July 2025, Google said Big Sleep had found another SQLite flaw that attackers were preparing to use, and it was fixed first. Defenders now have AI helpers too.
also: Big Sleep grew out of an earlier Project Zero experiment called Naptime.
Google described its 2024 results as highly experimental.
The 2025 flaw, CVE-2025-6965, was fixed in SQLite version 3.50.2.
wonders.think: If AI can find bugs, both defenders and attackers can use it. Who do you think gains more, and why?

wonders.title: In August 2024, the world got new locks for the quantum age
wonders.story: Today's internet locks depend on maths problems that normal computers cannot solve in any useful time. But a large quantum computer, a new kind of machine that uses the strange rules of tiny particles, could solve some of them quickly. Machines that big do not exist yet. Still, someone could record secret messages today and unlock them later. So in 2016, NIST, the US standards agency, asked the world's code experts for new methods. NIST studied 82 proposals from 25 countries, and experts tried to break them for years. On 13 August 2024, NIST published the first three finished standards: FIPS 203 for agreeing on secret keys, and FIPS 204 and 205 for digital signatures (ডিজিটাল স্বাক্ষর - a maths proof of who sent something). NIST told organisations to start switching as soon as possible.
also: FIPS 203 is based on a method called CRYSTALS-Kyber, now renamed ML-KEM.
FIPS 205 uses a different kind of maths, as a backup in case the main signature method is ever broken.
NIST also planned a fourth standard, FIPS 206, based on a method called FALCON.
wonders.think: Why would anyone spend years protecting against a machine that does not exist yet?

wonders.title: By December 2025, half of human web traffic used quantum-safe locks
wonders.story: New standards only help if people use them. When your browser opens a secure website, the two computers first agree on a secret key. Google Chrome began mixing a post-quantum method into this step, together with the classic one, so the connection stays safe if either method holds. In November 2024, Chrome 131 switched to ML-KEM, the method NIST had just standardised. Cloudflare, a company that carries a large part of the web's traffic, measured the change. At the start of 2025, about 29% of the human web traffic it saw used post-quantum key agreement. By early December 2025, it was 52%. A big jump came after September 2025, when Apple's iOS 26 turned it on by default for iPhones. Most people never noticed anything. Good defence is often invisible (অদৃশ্য - not seen).
also: Mixing an old and a new method together like this is called a hybrid approach.
Cloudflare reported that Kuwait's share rose from 13% to 37% during 2025, mostly thanks to iPhones.
Users did not need to install anything; the change came with normal browser and phone updates.
wonders.think: Is it good that the biggest security changes happen without people noticing, or should people be told?

wonders.title: Machines that find and fix bugs competed for a 4 million dollar prize
wonders.story: In August 2025, at the DEF CON security conference in Las Vegas, the US agency DARPA announced the winners of its AI Cyber Challenge. The goal was defence, not attack. Teams built AI systems that could find security bugs in open-source software and also write the fixes, with no humans helping during the test. The organisers hid 63 artificial bugs in real projects. The systems found 54 of them and fixed 43. They also found 18 real bugs that nobody knew about, which were reported to the people who maintain those projects. On average, a fix took about 45 minutes. First place and 4 million dollars went to Team Atlanta, which included researchers from Georgia Tech, Samsung and KAIST in Korea. All finalists agreed to release their systems as open source (ওপেন সোর্স - free for anyone to use and study).
also: Trail of Bits came second, winning 3 million dollars, and Theori came third with 1.5 million.
The average cost of the computing for each task was about 152 dollars.
Open-source software runs inside most phones and websites, so fixing it helps almost everyone.
wonders.think: If machines can fix bugs in 45 minutes, what jobs do you think human defenders will do in the future?

wonders.title: In July 2024, a security update itself crashed 8.5 million computers
wonders.story: On 19 July 2024, at 04:09 UTC, the security company CrowdStrike sent a small update to its Falcon software on Windows computers. Falcon runs deep inside the system to stop attackers. The update had a mistake. A new rule expected 21 pieces of information, but the program gave it only 20. When it tried to read the missing 21st item, it read outside its memory, and Windows crashed with a blue screen. The bad file was online for only 78 minutes, but Microsoft estimated that 8.5 million computers were hit, disrupting businesses around the world. It was not a cyberattack. CrowdStrike's fixes: send updates in stages (ধাপ - steps, one after another), starting with a small group of computers, test more kinds of input, and let customers choose when updates arrive.
also: Microsoft said the affected computers were less than 1% of all Windows machines.
Sending an update to a small test group first is called a canary release, after the birds miners once used to warn of danger.
CrowdStrike published its full root-cause report on 6 August 2024.
wonders.think: If safety tools can also cause accidents, how much power should we give them?

wonders.title: Every known security bug gets an ID number, like a library book
wonders.story: Imagine a thousand people talking about the same bug, but each calls it by a different name. Nobody could tell if they meant the same problem. In September 1999, the CVE list began to fix this. CVE stands for Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures. Each known vulnerability (দুর্বলতা - a weak spot) gets one ID, like CVE-2014-0160 for Heartbleed: the letters, the year, then a number. The list is run by MITRE, a US non-profit, with government money, and many companies are allowed to give out IDs for their own products. Now a defender in Dhaka and one in Toronto can say one ID and mean exactly the same bug. In April 2025 the funding almost ran out. The US government extended it at the last moment, and a new CVE Foundation was formed. The scare showed how much the world depends on one shared list.
also: Since 2015, the number after the year can have five or more digits, because so many bugs are found.
Companies such as Microsoft and Red Hat act as numbering authorities that give CVE IDs for their own products.
A separate score from 0 to 10 tells defenders how dangerous each CVE is.
wonders.think: Why might a shared name be one of the most important tools for people working together?

wonders.title: The padlock meant 'private', not 'safe', so Chrome took it away
wonders.story: When you visit a website, your messages travel through many computers on the way. Without protection, any of them could read or change what you send. HTTPS fixes this. Your browser and the website agree on a secret key and encrypt (এনক্রিপ্ট - scramble so only the right side can read) everything between you. A certificate proves the website really owns its name. For years, browsers showed a small padlock for HTTPS. In July 2018, Chrome 68 began marking plain HTTP sites as Not secure, and free certificates from Let's Encrypt made HTTPS easy for everyone. But a 2021 study found that only 11% of people knew what the padlock meant; many thought it meant a site was trustworthy. A scam site can use HTTPS too. So in 2023, Chrome 117 replaced the padlock with a plain settings icon.
also: Over 95% of pages loaded in Chrome on Windows use HTTPS.
HTTPS protects the road, not the destination: it does not tell you whether a website is honest.
Let's Encrypt is run by the Internet Security Research Group, a non-profit.
wonders.think: If a sign means something different from what people think, should we change the sign or teach the people?

wonders.title: A password manager keeps your secrets in a box it cannot open
wonders.story: A password manager stores all your passwords, so you only need to remember one: the master password. But if the company keeps your passwords on its servers, can it read them? With a good design, no. Your device turns your master password into a key by repeating a slow calculation hundreds of thousands of times. That key locks your vault (ভল্ট - a strong locked box) on your own device, before anything is sent. The company's servers only store scrambled data, and your master password itself never leaves your device. Bitwarden, one password manager, says even its own team cannot read your data. This design is often called zero-knowledge. There is one price: if you forget your master password, the company cannot recover it for you. So choose a long one that you will never forget.
also: Bitwarden repeats a method called PBKDF2 600,000 times by default, which makes guessing a master password very slow.
A password manager fills in a password only on the correct website, which helps protect you from fake look-alike sites.
Britain's National Cyber Security Centre recommends password managers, with two-step login turned on for the manager itself.
wonders.think: Is it safer to remember many weak passwords, or to trust one strong lock with all of them?

wonders.title: Why defenders fear a bug with zero days on the clock
wonders.story: When a security flaw is found, a clock starts. The software maker must understand it, write a fix, and send an update to users. A zero-day is a flaw the maker does not know about yet, so it has had zero days to fix it. If attackers find it first, nobody has a defence ready. Good researchers report a flaw privately to the maker and give them time. This is called coordinated disclosure (প্রকাশ - making something known). Google's Project Zero team usually gives 90 days. But if a flaw is already being used in real attacks, it gives only 7 days, because people are in danger now. In 2024, Google's threat experts counted 75 zero-days used in real attacks, fewer than the 98 they counted in 2023. The defence: find bugs before attackers do, and update quickly.
also: The term first meant software copied before its official release, on day zero.
Once a fix is released, attackers study it to find the flaw, so waiting to update is risky.
44% of the zero-days used in 2024 targeted products made for businesses.
wonders.think: Should a researcher ever make a flaw public before it is fixed? When might that be right or wrong?

wonders.title: Why Microsoft sends its biggest fixes on one Tuesday every month
wonders.story: Software always has bugs, and some of them are security holes. An update, also called a patch, closes them. But updates can break things too, so companies and schools need time to test them. In October 2003, after a fast-spreading worm called Blaster, Microsoft made a plan: release most security fixes together on the second Tuesday of each month. This became known as Patch Tuesday. Now admins (অ্যাডমিন - people who look after an organisation's computers) know when to get ready. Tuesday was chosen so there is time to fix problems before the weekend. There is a danger, though. Once a fix is public, attackers can study it and attack computers that have not updated. Some people call the next day Exploit Wednesday. The lesson: install updates soon, because the race starts when the fix appears.
also: Other companies, such as SAP, Adobe and Oracle, release some of their fixes on the same day.
WannaCry in 2017 hit computers that had missed a Patch Tuesday fix released two months earlier.
On Linux Mint, the Update Manager does a similar job for your system and your apps.
wonders.think: Should updates install by themselves, or should people choose when? What are the risks of each?

wonders.title: How your phone and a website make the same secret code every 30 seconds
wonders.story: Many accounts can ask for a second step after your password: a short code from an app on your phone, usually six digits. But how does the website know the right code, when your phone is not even talking to it? When you set it up, the website shows you a QR code. It holds a shared secret (গোপন চাবি - secret key) that is now saved in two places: on the website's server and in your app. After that, both sides do the same calculation. They mix the secret with the current time, counted in 30-second steps, and turn the result into a short number. Same secret plus same time gives the same code. This method is called TOTP, and it was published as an internet standard in May 2011. Even if someone steals your password, they still need the code from your phone.
also: The app works even with no internet, because it only needs the secret and the clock.
If your phone's clock is very wrong, the codes may not match.
TOTP is built on an older method, HOTP, which used a counter instead of the time.
